topics.name: Place Value and Rounding
topics.learning_target: I can read, write, model, compare, and round numbers up to 10,000.
success_criteria: Identify each digit's value (e.g., in 4,582 the 5 means 500).
Represent a number using base-ten models.
Write numbers in standard, word, and expanded form.
Compare numbers using >, <, = correctly.
Round numbers to the nearest ten or hundred using place value reasoning.
topics.topic_focus: Understanding place value up to 10,000 and rounding to the nearest ten and hundred
topics.ald_focus: ALD Level 3 In-Class Practice only (not homework column)

lessons.title: Place Value to the Thousands
lessons.focus: Understanding the value of each digit in a 4-digit number.
lessons.learning_goal: I can explain the value of each digit in a number up to 10,000.
success_criteria: Identify the value of each digit in a 4-digit number.
Represent the number using base-ten models.
Write the number in expanded form correctly.
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Students explain the value of each digit based on its place, and understand zero as a placeholder.
lessons.benchmark_example: “The 5 in 4,582 is in the hundreds place, so it represents 500, not 5.”
lessons.sentence_frame: The __ is in the __ place, so it means __.

misconceptions.misconception: Reads the digit instead of its value
misconceptions.fix: Build with base-ten blocks and label each place; say “6 hundreds,” not “6.”
Model expanded form on a place-value chart with blocks.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Review 2nd-grade place value to hundreds (MA.2.NSO.1.1). Flash 3-digit numbers (e.g., 348) and ask “What is the value of the 4?” (40). Then extend: “What happens when we add a digit in front — 3,048?”
lessons.i_do: Model with 3,476. Build it with base-ten blocks (3 thousand-cubes, 4 flats, 7 rods, 6 units). Think aloud: “The 3 is in the thousands place, so it means 3,000. The 4 is in the hundreds place, so it means 400…” Record it on a place-value chart, then expanded form: 3,476 = 3,000 + 400 + 70 + 6.
lessons.we_do: Together, build 5,281. Call on students to place each digit on the chart and state its value using the frame “The __ is in the __ place, so it means __.” Turn-and-talk: partner A builds, partner B checks each digit's value (MTR 4.1).
cfu: Write the value of the underlined digit: 5,3̩3 → the 3
lessons.you_do: Represent 2,861 three ways: place-value chart, expanded form, and one sentence explaining the value of a digit you choose.

cpa.concrete:
Build 3,476 with base-ten blocks:
🟦🟦🟦 thousands   🟩🟩🟩🟩 hundreds   🟨🟨🟨🟨🟨🟨🟨 tens   ⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜ ones
cpa.pictorial: Place-value chart — Th 3 | H 4 | T 7 | O 6

lessons.level3_example: “The 7 is in the tens place, which means 70, because each ten is worth ten ones.”

exit_ticket.problem: What is the value of the 8 in 8,145?

lessons.title: Read & Write Numbers in Standard, Word & Expanded Form
lessons.focus: Writing numbers in multiple forms; zero as a placeholder.
lessons.learning_goal: I can write a number in standard form, word form, and expanded form.
success_criteria: Read a 4-digit number correctly.
Write the same number in standard, word, and expanded form.
Use zero as a placeholder correctly.
lessons.success_example: 4,209 → Standard: 4,209 · Word: four thousand two hundred nine · Expanded: 4,000 + 200 + 9.
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Students understand zero as a placeholder and do not use “and” in whole-number word form.
lessons.benchmark_example: In 4,209 the 0 shows there are no tens; it is written but not said as a word.

misconceptions.example: Writes “four thousand two hundred and nine”
misconceptions.fix: There is no “and” in whole-number word form; “and” is used for decimals.

misconceptions.misconception: Runs digits together / drops a place
misconceptions.fix: Write one place at a time using the place-value chart.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Quick review of 7.1: show 4,582 and have students state each digit's value, then say the number aloud correctly (“four thousand five hundred eighty-two”).
lessons.i_do: Model with 3,067. Build with place-value disks. Write standard (3,067), word (three thousand sixty-seven), and expanded (3,000 + 60 + 7). Think aloud about the 0: “There are no hundreds, so I hold the place with a 0 — but I don't say it in word form.”
lessons.we_do: Together convert 4,209 into all three forms, emphasizing zero as a placeholder. Students whisper-read the word form to a partner and write the expanded form on whiteboards to hold up.
cfu: Write “three thousand eight” in standard form
lessons.you_do: Convert 7,026 into standard form, word form, and expanded form.

cpa.concrete: Place-value disks: 3 in thousands, 0 in hundreds, 6 in tens, 7 in ones.
cpa.pictorial: Place-value chart — Th 3 | H 0 | T 6 | O 7

lessons.level3_example: “I needed a 0 in the hundreds place to show there are no hundreds, but I don't say ‘zero’ when I read it.”

lessons.title: Model & Represent Numbers (Base-Ten Models)
lessons.focus: Representing numbers up to 10,000 using models, pictures, and place value charts.
lessons.learning_goal: I can represent a 4-digit number with base-ten models, drawings, and a place-value chart.
success_criteria: Build numbers using base-ten materials.
Draw visual models (flats, rods, cubes) that match each digit's value.
Connect models to the place-value chart and expanded form.
lessons.benchmark_clarification: The model must match the value of each digit; each group is labeled with its place value.
lessons.benchmark_example: For 2,547, draw 2 thousand-cubes, 5 flats, 4 rods, 7 units and label 1,000 / 100 / 10 / 1.

misconceptions.misconception: Mislabels the value of a drawn model
misconceptions.example: Draws 5 flats but calls it “5” instead of 500
misconceptions.fix: Label each model piece with its place value (100, 10).

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Show a place-value chart with 2,547 and have students sketch quick base-ten pictures for a 3-digit warm-up (e.g., 253) to practice drawing flats, rods, and units.
lessons.i_do: Model 4,283: build with blocks, then draw a quick picture (squares = thousands, flats = hundreds, lines = tens, dots = ones), then connect to the chart and expanded form. Think aloud matching each piece to its value.
lessons.we_do: Together represent 3,709. Highlight the 0 hundreds — no flats drawn. Students build with a partner and label each group with its value (1,000, 100, 10, 1).
cfu: Build and represent 3,709 as a chart, a quick picture, and expanded form
lessons.you_do: Represent 5,682 three ways: a drawn base-ten model, a place-value chart, and expanded form.

cpa.concrete:
Build 4,543 with blocks:
🟥🟥🟥🟥 = 4 thousands   🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 = 5 hundreds   🟨🟨🟨🟨 = 4 tens   ⬜⬜⬜ = 3 ones
cpa.pictorial: Place-value chart — TH 4 | H 5 | T 4 | O 3

lessons.level3_example: “4 thousands means 4,000 because each thousand is ten hundreds.”

exit_ticket.problem: Which model shows 4,201? Circle the correct base-ten picture.

lessons.title: Compare Numbers to 10,000 Using >, <, =
lessons.learning_goal: I can compare numbers up to 10,000 using >, <, and =.
success_criteria: Compare thousands → hundreds → tens → ones, in order.
Justify the comparison using place value.
lessons.success_example: 3,842 > 3,624 because 8 hundreds > 6 hundreds (the thousands are equal).
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Comparisons are based on place value — start from the largest place (left) and find the first place where the digits differ.
lessons.benchmark_example: 7,214 > 6,998 because 7 thousands > 6 thousands, even though 6,998 has larger later digits.
lessons.sentence_frame: I compared the __ place and saw __ > __, so __ __ __.

misconceptions.fix: Always compare from left to right (largest place first).

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks a bigger first digit means bigger
misconceptions.fix: Align digits on a place-value chart; more places = greater.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Review comparison symbols with 2-digit numbers (the symbol “opens” toward the larger number). Ask: “How do we decide which is bigger when numbers have 4 digits?”
lessons.i_do: Model comparing 4,752 and 4,529. Line them up on a place-value chart. Think aloud: “Thousands are equal (4 = 4). Move to hundreds: 7 > 5, so 4,752 > 4,529.” Stress starting from the LEFT (largest place).
lessons.we_do: Together compare 6,201 and 6,128. Students find the first place where digits differ and justify with the frame. Use thumbs signals for >, <, =.
lessons.you_do: Compare 7,432 ___ 7,423 and write a sentence justifying your answer using place value.

cpa.concrete: Build both numbers with blocks side by side and compare the largest place first.
cpa.pictorial: Two rows of a place-value chart aligned vertically.

lessons.level3_example: “Since the thousands are equal, I compared the hundreds: 7 hundreds > 5 hundreds, so 4,752 > 4,529.”

lessons.title: Round to Nearest Ten
lessons.focus: Rounding to the nearest 10 using the ones digit.
lessons.learning_goal: I can round a number to the nearest ten.
success_criteria: Identify the two tens the number is between.
Use the ones digit to decide round up or round down.
lessons.success_example: 47 → 50 (ones digit 7 is ≥ 5, round up); 42 → 40 (ones digit 2 is < 5, round down).
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Rounding to the nearest ten uses the ONES digit; 5 rounds up.
lessons.benchmark_example: 45 is the midpoint between 40 and 50, so 45 rounds up to 50.
lessons.sentence_frame: __ is closer to __ than __, so it rounds to __.

misconceptions.example: Uses the tens digit to round to the nearest ten
misconceptions.fix: To round to the nearest ten, look at the ONES digit.
5 means round UP; show 65 at the midpoint on a number line.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Skip-count by 10s (10, 20, 30…). Show a number line from 40 to 50 and ask which tens 47 sits between.
lessons.i_do: Model rounding 47. Place it on a 40–50 number line and mark the midpoint 45. Think aloud: “47 is past 45, so it's closer to 50 → 47 rounds to 50.” State the rule (ones ≥ 5 round up, < 5 round down). Then round 42 → 40.
lessons.we_do: Together round 63, 28, and 94 on a number line. Students place each number, find the midpoint, and decide up or down using the sentence frame.
lessons.you_do: Round 57 to the nearest ten and explain why, using the number line.

cpa.concrete: Build the number with cubes; walk it to the nearest ten on a floor number-line tape.
cpa.pictorial: Number line 40–50 with the midpoint 45 marked.
cpa.abstract: If ones ≥ 5 → round up; if ones < 5 → round down. 47 → 50

lessons.level3_example: “47 is closer to 50 than 40, so it rounds to 50 — the ones digit 7 is more than 5.”

lessons.title: Round to Nearest Hundred
lessons.focus: Rounding to the nearest 100 using the tens digit.
lessons.learning_goal: I can round a number to the nearest hundred.
success_criteria: Identify which two hundreds the number is between.
Use the tens digit to decide round up or round down.
lessons.success_example: 378 → 400 (tens digit 7 is ≥ 5, round up); 612 → 600 (tens digit 1 is < 5, round down).
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Rounding to the nearest hundred uses the TENS digit.
lessons.benchmark_example: 378 is between 300 and 400; the tens digit 7 is ≥ 5, so it rounds up to 400.
lessons.sentence_frame: __ is between __ and __; the tens digit is __, so it rounds to __.

misconceptions.misconception: Uses the ones digit to round to the nearest hundred
misconceptions.fix: To round to the nearest hundred, look at the TENS digit.

misconceptions.misconception: Rounds down when the tens digit is 5
misconceptions.fix: A tens digit of 5 rounds UP: 950 → 1,000.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Skip-count by 100s. Review 7.5: which digit rounds to the nearest ten? (ones) Predict: “Which digit do we use for the nearest hundred?”
lessons.i_do: Model rounding 378. Place it between 300 and 400; mark the midpoint 350. Think aloud: “378 is past 350 → closer to 400. The tens digit 7 is ≥ 5, so round up → 400.”
lessons.we_do: Together round 612 and 841. Students name the two hundreds each is between and use the tens digit to decide, using the sentence frame.
lessons.you_do: Round 729 to the nearest hundred and explain which two hundreds it is between.

cpa.concrete: Locate the number on a number line marked in 100 intervals.
cpa.abstract: If tens ≥ 5 → round up; if tens < 5 → round down. 378 → 400

lessons.level3_example: “612 rounds to 600 because the tens digit is 1, which is less than 5, so I round down.”

lessons.title: Problem Solving with Place Value & Rounding
lessons.focus: Estimate, calculate, and check reasonableness in real-world problems.
lessons.learning_goal: I can use place value and rounding to estimate and solve real-world problems.
success_criteria: Estimate by rounding to the nearest ten or hundred.
Solve and then check whether the answer is reasonable.
lessons.success_example: There are 3,287 people in the stadium → about 3,300 to the nearest hundred (tens digit 8 rounds up).
lessons.benchmark_clarification: Use estimate → calculate → check reasonableness; round to the place the problem asks for.
lessons.benchmark_example: Round 3,287 to the nearest hundred: tens digit 8 ≥ 5 → 3,300; then confirm 3,300 is close to 3,287.
lessons.sentence_frame: I rounded __ to the nearest __ to estimate, and __ is reasonable because __.

misconceptions.misconception: Rounds to the wrong place in a word problem
misconceptions.example: Rounds 3,287 to 3,290 when asked for the nearest hundred
misconceptions.fix: Underline “nearest hundred”; use the tens digit.
Compare the estimate back to the original — it should be close.

lessons.activate_prior_knowledge: Review the rounding rules from 7.5–7.6 (ones digit → nearest ten; tens digit → nearest hundred). Ask when estimating is useful in real life (crowds, money, distance).
lessons.i_do: Model: “There are 3,287 people in the stadium. About how many is that to the nearest hundred?” Think aloud: tens digit 8 ≥ 5 → round up → 3,300. Then check: “Is 3,300 close to 3,287? Yes.”
lessons.we_do: Together solve: “A store sold 1,564 stickers. About how many to the nearest hundred?” Students estimate first, then justify using estimate → calculate → check reasonableness.
cfu: Is 3,300 a reasonable estimate for 3,287? Explain.
lessons.you_do: A library has 2,438 books. About how many to the nearest hundred? Show your rounding and explain why the estimate is reasonable.

cpa.concrete: Model the quantity with grouped materials or locate it on a number line for estimation.
cpa.pictorial: Number line to place the number between benchmark hundreds.
cpa.abstract: 3,287 → 3,300 (nearest hundred); estimate, then verify against the real number

lessons.level3_example: “I rounded 3,287 to the nearest hundred because it makes the number easier to use, and 3,300 is close to the real number, so my estimate is reasonable.”

exit_ticket.problem: A store sold 1,564 stickers. About how many is that to the nearest hundred?

topics.name: Understand Fractions (Chapter 9)
success_criteria: identify a unit fraction.
explain how equal parts are used to name and write
model fractions less than or greater than 1.
describe a fraction as a sum of unit fractions.
